title: Chunking 101
description: Turn documents into retrievable units while preserving meaning.
outcomes: Explain why chunking dominates retrieval quality in most RAG systems.
Choose a baseline chunking strategy and know when overlap helps.
Recognize common chunking failure modes and how to debug them.
searchText: Chunking 101 Turn documents into retrievable units while preserving meaning. pre-retrieval foundations chunking retrieval Explain why chunking dominates retrieval quality in most RAG systems. Choose a baseline chunking strategy and know when overlap helps. Recognize common chunking failure modes and how to debug them. Goals - Understand why chunking exists (and why it’s so often the root cause). - Learn two baseline chunking strategies you can ship. - Learn how to spot “bad chunking” in logs when retrieval fails. Prereqs - Read: **Tokenizers & Context Windows** (token budgets drive chunk size decisions). Core idea Why chunking matters In RAG you don’t retrieve entire documents—you retrieve **chunks**. Good chunking: - keeps semantic units together - stays within token budgets - makes retrieval precise Bad chunking: - splits definitions from the thing they define - mixes multiple topics - causes “almost relevant” context that confuses the model Two simple strategies 1. **Fixed-size chunking**: easiest to implement, often “good enough” to start. 2. **Overlap**: reduces boundary loss (but increases index size). Failure modes - **Too small**: definitions split from what they define → fragments get retrieved. - **Too large**: irrelevant text dilutes relevance → context rot + token waste. - **Wrong boundaries**: splitting in the middle of a table, list, or code block. - **No traceability**: missing chunk IDs / source mapping → impossible to debug. Production defaults - Start with **300–600 tokens** per chunk, **10–20% overlap**. - Prefer structure-aware splitting when you have headings (Markdown/PDF sections). - Always store: `doc_id`, stable `chunk_id`, section/page metadata. Canonical reference: - Production RAG Blueprint - RAG Techniques Encyclopedia Do next

title: Embedding Fundamentals
description: Vectors, similarity, and why embeddings make retrieval possible.
outcomes: Explain what embeddings are and why they enable semantic retrieval.
Differentiate similarity vs distance metrics (and when they matter).
Know the common production failure modes (model mismatch, vectors-only, bad chunking).
searchText: Embedding Fundamentals Vectors, similarity, and why embeddings make retrieval possible. foundations foundations embeddings vectors similarity Explain what embeddings are and why they enable semantic retrieval. Differentiate similarity vs distance metrics (and when they matter). Know the common production failure modes (model mismatch, vectors-only, bad chunking). Goals - Build the correct intuition for "meaning as geometry". - Understand why similarity math matters, but isn't the main bottleneck. - Be ready to implement the primitives used by vector databases. Prereqs - Read: **Why RAG Exists** (`/learn/phase-0/why-rag-exists`). Core idea What is an embedding? An **embedding** maps content (text, image, code) into a vector of numbers: - similar meaning → vectors are close - different meaning → vectors are far This turns "search for meaning" into a geometry problem. Similarity vs distance You'll see both in practice: - **Cosine similarity** (most common for embeddings) - **Dot product** (often used directly, especially if vectors are normalized) - **Euclidean distance** (good for intuition; less common for modern text embeddings) Retrieval quality often depends more on chunking + query formulation than the exact similarity metric. BERT vs Sentence Transformers: A Critical Distinction Understanding the difference between BERT and Sentence Transformers is essential for RAG. Token-Level vs Sentence-Level Embeddings | Aspect | BERT | Sentence Transformers | | ---------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------- | | **Embedding Output** | One vector per token | One vector per sentence | | **Training Objective** | Masked word prediction + NSP | Semantic similarity | | **Network Structure** | Single encoder | Siamese/Triplet networks | | **Best For** | NER, token classification | Semantic search, retrieval | Why BERT's [CLS] Token Fails for Retrieval BERT's `[CLS]` token was trained for Next Sentence Prediction, not semantic similarity. Two sentences with different meanings can have similar `[CLS]` embeddings. How Sentence Transformers Fix This Sentence Transformers modify BERT with: 1. **Siamese Network Training**: Train on sentence pairs to learn similarity 2. **Contrastive Loss**: Push dissimilar sentences apart 3. **Mean Pooling**: Average all tokens instead of just `[CLS]` Training Data Difference | Training Data | BERT | Sentence Transformers | | ------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------- | | **Corpus** | Wikipedia, Books (MLM) | SNLI, MultiNLI (sentence pairs) | | **Signal** | Predict missing words | Are sentences similar? | | **Result** | Understands words in context | Understands sentence meaning | For RAG, **always use Sentence Transformers** or API embeddings (OpenAI, Cohere). Never use raw BERT `[CLS]` embeddings for retrieval. Failure modes - **Vectors-only retrieval**: you will miss exact terms (IDs/acronyms) unless you use hybrid retrieval. - **Model mismatch**: query and docs embedded with different models → similarity becomes meaningless. - **Wrong chunking**: embeddings can't recover lost structure (garbage in → garbage out). - **Using raw BERT for retrieval**: The `[CLS]` token was not trained for similarity. Production defaults - Choose one good baseline embedding model and evaluate changes with Recall@k. - Prefer **hybrid + reranking** improvements before fine-tuning embeddings. - Use Compare when choosing models: - Compare: Embeddings Do next

title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Decision Framework
description: When to use retrieval, when to fine-tune, and how to combine both.
outcomes: Compare RAG and fine-tuning across multiple dimensions
Make informed architecture decisions based on your use case
Understand how to combine both approaches effectively
searchText: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Decision Framework When to use retrieval, when to fine-tune, and how to combine both. foundations architecture fine-tuning decision-framework strategy Compare RAG and fine-tuning across multiple dimensions Make informed architecture decisions based on your use case Understand how to combine both approaches effectively Goals - Understand the fundamental differences between RAG and fine-tuning. - Apply a decision framework to choose the right approach. - Learn when to combine both for optimal results. Prereqs - **Why RAG Exists** (Phase 0). - Basic understanding of LLM training concepts. Core idea Two main ways to give LLMs specialized knowledge: | Approach | How It Works | | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | **RAG** | Retrieve relevant docs at query time, add to prompt | | **Fine-Tuning** | Train the model's weights on your data | Neither is universally better—the right choice depends on your specific needs. --- The Decision Framework Dimension 1: What Are You Trying to Achieve? **Key insight from Microsoft Research:** - RAG provides **factual, access-controlled, timely information** - Fine-tuning adapts **style, tone, and vocabulary** Dimension 2: How Often Does Your Data Change? | Data Update Frequency | Best Approach | Why | | ----------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------- | | **Real-time** (seconds) | RAG | Fine-tuning can't keep up | | **Daily/Weekly** | RAG | Easy to update index | | **Monthly** | Either | Both feasible | | **Rarely/Never** | Fine-tuning | Worth the upfront cost | Dimension 3: Cost and Infrastructure | Factor | RAG | Fine-Tuning | | ------------------ | ---------------------------- | ----------------------- | | **Upfront cost** | Low (just indexing) | High (training) | | **Per-query cost** | Higher (retrieval + context) | Lower (no retrieval) | | **Latency** | +50-200ms for retrieval | Minimal overhead | | **Infrastructure** | Vector DB required | Training infrastructure | | **Updates** | Re-index specific docs | Full retraining | Dimension 4: Use Case Characteristics | Characteristic | → RAG | → Fine-Tuning | | -------------------------- | ----- | ------------- | | Need citations/sources | ✓ | | | Access control per user | ✓ | | | Large knowledge base | ✓ | | | Consistent output format | | ✓ | | Domain-specific vocabulary | | ✓ | | Reasoning patterns | | ✓ | | Reduce hallucination | ✓ | | --- Decision Flowchart --- Combining RAG + Fine-Tuning For many production systems, the best approach is **RAG first, then fine-tune**. The Optimal Workflow Case Study: Agriculture QA System From Microsoft's research: | Configuration | Accuracy | | -------------------- | -------------- | | Base GPT-4 | 47% | | Fine-tuned GPT-4 | 53% (+6%) | | RAG only | 52% (+5%) | | **Fine-tuned + RAG** | **58% (+11%)** | The combination outperforms either approach alone. --- Comparison Table | Dimension | RAG | Fine-Tuning | | ------------------ | --------------------- | -------------------- | | **Best for** | Factual knowledge | Behavioral change | | **Data freshness** | Up-to-date | Point-in-time | | **Cost model** | Per-query (retrieval) | Upfront (training) | | **Update speed** | Minutes | Hours/Days | | **Hallucination** | Lower (grounded) | Higher (memorized) | | **Citations** | Easy (source docs) | Hard (no provenance) | | **Latency** | +retrieval time | Minimal | | **Access control** | Per-user possible | All-or-nothing | | **Implementation** | Moderate | Complex | --- Common Patterns Pattern 1: RAG for Knowledge, Fine-Tune for Format Pattern 2: Fine-Tune for Reasoning, RAG for Facts Pattern 3: Fine-Tune for Efficiency --- Failure modes ❌ "We'll just fine-tune on everything" Fine-tuning on facts leads to stale, hallucinated responses. - **Fix**: Use fine-tuning for behavior, RAG for facts. ❌ Skipping RAG because "fine-tuning is more powerful" Fine-tuning cannot solve the freshness problem. - **Fix**: RAG first, fine-tune later for style. ❌ Over-engineering before validation Building complex hybrid systems before proving value. - **Fix**: Start with basic RAG, measure, then optimize. --- Production defaults | Scenario | Recommendation | | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | **MVP/Prototype** | RAG only | | **Production v1** | RAG with basic prompting | | **Production v2** | RAG + fine-tuned for format/style | | **High-volume** | Fine-tune to reduce context → lower cost | | **Domain-specific** | Fine-tune for terminology + RAG for facts | **Start with RAG.** Fine-tune only after you have a working RAG system and clear evidence of what fine-tuning would improve. --- Do next - title: Tokenizers & Context Windows
description: Why chunking exists: models read tokens, not characters.
outcomes: Explain why tokens (not characters) determine context limits and cost.
Recognize why chunking is necessary even with long-context models.
Adopt the production habit: measure tokens, don’t guess.
searchText: Tokenizers & Context Windows Why chunking exists: models read tokens, not characters. foundations foundations tokenization context-window Explain why tokens (not characters) determine context limits and cost. Recognize why chunking is necessary even with long-context models. Adopt the production habit: measure tokens, don’t guess. Goals - Understand what a token is (and why it’s not a word). - Know how context windows constrain chunk size and “top‑k into prompt”. - Build the habit of token budgeting early. Prereqs - Read: **Embedding Fundamentals**. Core idea Tokens ≠ words LLMs operate on **tokens**. A token is *not* always a word: - `"hello"` might be 1 token - `"unbelievable"` might be multiple tokens - punctuation and whitespace matter That’s why prompt length and chunk size matter. Use a token counter in production. “~4 chars per token” is a rough heuristic, not a guarantee. Failure modes - **Character counting**: using char length instead of tokens → unpredictable truncation and cost. - **Over-retrieval**: retrieving too many chunks because you didn’t budget tokens. - **Ignoring formatting**: code/tables can token-bloat and crowd out useful context. Production defaults - Always compute token counts for: - chunk sizes - retrieved context size - system prompt + instructions - Prefer “retrieve candidates → rerank → keep 5–10” over “dump everything”. Do next

outcomes: Understand the learning loop (Learn → Challenge → Compare → Ship).

searchText: Welcome to RAG Academy How this platform works: learn → build → compare → specialize. foundations foundations meta learning Understand the learning loop (Learn → Challenge → Compare → Ship). Know where to start and how to avoid getting overwhelmed. Use challenges as the primary way to learn (not passive reading). Read the lesson, then immediately do the linked coding challenge(s). You’ll learn RAG fastest by implementing the primitives yourself. Goals - Learn how to navigate the platform without getting lost. - Internalize the “build order”: fundamentals → retrieval → rerank → safety → eval → harden. - Treat challenges as the primary learning unit. Prereqs None. Core idea We optimize for **production competence**, not passive watching: - **Code-first**: every concept has a challenge. - **Failure-mode driven**: you’ll learn why systems break, not just the “happy path”. - **From scratch → production**: implement the core algorithm, then learn the real-world constraints. The learning loop: 1. **Learn** the concept (short lesson) 2. **Build** the primitive (challenge) 3. **Measure** (tests + later: retrieval metrics + groundedness checks) 4. **Iterate** (hints + debugging tools) Failure modes - **Reading without building**: you will *feel* like you understand but won’t be able to debug real systems. - **Random technique hopping**: you’ll collect methods without knowing when to use them. - **Skipping measurement**: you’ll “improve” the system without knowing if it got better. Production defaults - Follow the Study Plan for the default sequence: baseline retrieval → hybrid → rerank → context shaping → safety → eval. - Use Compare pages when you’re stuck choosing between tools/techniques. Do next In this phase you’ll learn the minimal pieces that every RAG system needs: - vectors + similarity - chunking - basic retrieval - prompting patterns Then read: **Why RAG Exists** → `/learn/phase-0/why-rag-exists`.

title: Why RAG Exists
description: LLMs are great at language, but not at truth. RAG reduces hallucinations by grounding answers in your data.
outcomes: Explain the three core LLM limitations: cutoff, hallucination, privacy.
Describe RAG as non‑parametric memory and where it fits (offline vs online).
Recognize why retrieval quality is the first thing to debug.
searchText: Why RAG Exists LLMs are great at language, but not at truth. RAG reduces hallucinations by grounding answers in your data. foundations foundations rag grounding hallucinations Explain the three core LLM limitations: cutoff, hallucination, privacy. Describe RAG as non‑parametric memory and where it fits (offline vs online). Recognize why retrieval quality is the first thing to debug. Goals - Understand why “LLM + prompt” is not enough for truth and freshness. - Learn the mental model: **parametric vs non‑parametric memory**. - Know what you should build first (and what to ignore early). Prereqs - Read: **Welcome to RAG Academy** (optional) for how to use the platform. Core idea RAG = **Retrieve** relevant context from your documents, then **Generate** an answer using that context. The problem RAG solves Large Language Models (LLMs) can: - Write fluent text - Generalize across tasks - Reason *sometimes* But they also: - **Hallucinate** (confidently produce incorrect details) - Have **stale knowledge** (their training cutoff) - Can't reliably access your **private / fresh** data The core architecture: parametric vs non-parametric memory LLMs are **parametric memory** systems: they compress knowledge into fixed weights. - **Knowledge cutoff**: training data becomes stale. - **Hallucination**: fluent text ≠ truth. - **Privacy**: your internal data isn’t accessible unless you provide it. RAG adds **non‑parametric memory**: an external store you can update, permission, and debug. Minimal pipeline 1. **Chunk** documents 2. **Embed** chunks into vectors 3. **Retrieve** top-k chunks for a query 4. **Prompt** the LLM with the retrieved context Offline vs online (production reality) In production you separate **offline indexing** from **online query time**. - **Offline**: parse → chunk → metadata → embed → store - **Online**: query → retrieve candidates → rerank → shape context → generate + cite/refuse If you want the full end‑to‑end pipeline (and the knobs that matter), use the blueprint as your canonical reference: - Production RAG Blueprint Failure modes - **Prompt-first debugging**: trying to “prompt your way out” when the right evidence isn’t retrieved. - **Vectors-only retrieval**: missing exact terms (IDs, acronyms) that BM25/hybrid would catch. - **Over-retrieval**: k too high → context rot → the model ignores key evidence. Production defaults - Start with **hybrid retrieval + reranking** as your production baseline. - Keep contexts small: retrieve 20–50 → rerank → keep 5–10 → cite everything. Canonical reference (don’t memorize): - Production RAG Blueprint Do next Go to **Challenges** and implement: - Dot product - Cosine similarity - Euclidean distance Then we’ll connect those primitives into a tiny retriever.

title: Your First RAG (Minimal Pipeline)
description: A tiny end-to-end retrieval + prompt pipeline (without external APIs yet).
outcomes: Describe the minimal end-to-end RAG loop and where it fails.
Apply grounding rules: cite sources or refuse when evidence is missing.

searchText: Your First RAG (Minimal Pipeline) A tiny end-to-end retrieval + prompt pipeline (without external APIs yet). retrieval foundations rag retrieval prompting Describe the minimal end-to-end RAG loop and where it fails. Apply grounding rules: cite sources or refuse when evidence is missing. Know what to implement next: hybrid retrieval, reranking, and evaluation. Goals - Build the smallest RAG loop that still teaches correct production instincts. - Learn the “grounded answer” rule: cite evidence or refuse. - Understand what to add next (hybrid retrieval, reranking, eval). Prereqs - Read: **Why RAG Exists**, **Embedding Fundamentals**, **Tokenizers & Context**, **Chunking 101**. Core idea The minimal RAG pipeline Even “hello world RAG” has the same structure as production: 1. Prepare chunks (+ optional metadata) 2. Retrieve top-k chunks for a query 3. Build a prompt that forces grounding If the right evidence isn’t in your top‑k, no amount of prompt engineering will save you. Treat retrieval quality as an engineering problem: log it, measure it, iterate it. This lesson is about building the minimal pipeline. For the full production pipeline (offline vs online, technique menu, and the knobs that matter), use: Production RAG Blueprint RAG Techniques Encyclopedia In the MVP we’ll avoid paid embedding APIs by using simple vector primitives and toy embeddings. Later we’ll add real embedding providers. Failure modes - **Wrong evidence in top‑k**: the model answers confidently using irrelevant chunks. - **Over-retrieval**: too many chunks → lost-in-the-middle → model ignores the key line. - **Prompt injection**: retrieved content contains instructions → the model follows them unless you treat sources as untrusted. Production defaults - Retrieval: **hybrid + RRF** → rerank candidates → keep 5–10. - Context shaping: dedupe, token budget, attention-aware ordering. - Grounding: citations by chunk id; refusal if evidence is missing. title: Context Shaping
description: Turn retrieved chunks into an effective prompt context.
outcomes: Explain why chunk order and formatting affect answer quality.
Implement lost-in-the-middle mitigation and context compression.
Know when to truncate vs. when to rerank more aggressively.
searchText: Context Shaping Turn retrieved chunks into an effective prompt context. post-retrieval post-retrieval context-shaping compression ordering Explain why chunk order and formatting affect answer quality. Implement lost-in-the-middle mitigation and context compression. Know when to truncate vs. when to rerank more aggressively. Goals - Understand why retrieval is not enough—how you present context matters. - Learn three context shaping techniques: ordering, compression, formatting. - Know your token budget and how to stay within it. Prereqs - Read: **Query Transforms** (you should have good retrievals first). - Read: **Tokenizers & Context Windows** (token budgets are central here). Core idea The context problem You've retrieved 10 relevant chunks. Now what? Simply concatenating them causes issues: - **Lost in the middle**: LLMs attend poorly to middle content. - **Token overflow**: exceeding context window truncates important info. - **Irrelevant noise**: low-relevance chunks dilute good evidence. Three shaping techniques **1. Ordering (Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation)** Place the most relevant chunks at the **start** and **end** of context: Research shows LLMs attend better to the edges of their context. **2. Compression** Reduce token count while preserving meaning: - **Extractive**: keep only relevant sentences from each chunk - **Abstractive**: summarize each chunk into key points - **LLMLingua-style**: use a small model to remove filler tokens Compression can reduce context by 50-70% with minimal quality loss. **3. Formatting** Structure context for the LLM: Clear formatting helps the LLM cite correctly and reduces hallucination. Token budget math Failure modes - **Over-compression**: removing content that was actually needed. - **Wrong ordering**: burying the best evidence in the middle. - **Format confusion**: inconsistent formatting leads to citation errors. - **Token underutilization**: being too conservative, missing evidence. Production defaults - Rerank to top-5/top-10 before shaping (garbage in → garbage out). - Apply lost-in-the-middle ordering: best at start and end. - Keep total context under 8k-16k tokens even if model supports more. - Add clear source markers for citation grounding. Canonical reference: - RAG Techniques Encyclopedia - Compare: Reranking Do next

Goals - Understand the two-part evaluation problem: retrieval + generation. - Learn to build and use a golden set. - Know which metrics to track and when. Prereqs - Read: **Grounding & Safety** (you should have a working, safe pipeline). - Complete at least one challenge in the Evaluation track. Core idea Why evaluate? Without measurement, you're guessing: - "I think it got better" → confirmation bias. - "Users seem happy" → survivorship bias. - "It works on my examples" → overfitting. Evaluation turns intuition into evidence. Two evaluation layers **1. Retrieval Evaluation** Does the system find the right chunks? | Metric | What it measures | |--------|------------------| | Recall@k | Did we find all relevant chunks in top-k? | | Precision@k | What fraction of top-k is relevant? | | MRR | How early does the first relevant chunk appear? | | nDCG | Weighted score considering position | **2. Generation Evaluation** Does the LLM use context correctly? | Metric | What it measures | |--------|------------------| | Faithfulness | Are claims supported by context? | | Answer Relevance | Does the answer address the question? | | Context Recall | Is the answer derivable from context? | Building a golden set A golden set is a collection of (query, expected_sources) pairs: Start with 25-50 queries covering: - Common questions (high traffic). - Edge cases (where you've seen failures). - Diverse topics (coverage). The evaluation workflow Failure modes - **Teaching to the test**: optimizing for golden set, missing real queries. - **Metric gaming**: improving one metric at the expense of others. - **Stale golden sets**: queries that no longer reflect real usage. - **LLM judge inconsistency**: different runs give different scores. Production defaults - Build golden set from real user queries (logs). - Track retrieval metrics first (garbage in → garbage out). - Use multiple runs for LLM-based metrics (variance is high). - Refresh golden set quarterly as usage evolves. - Set regression alerts: notify if metrics drop > 5%. title: Grounding & Safety
description: Ensure answers are faithful to sources and defend against abuse.
outcomes: Explain the difference between hallucination and fabrication in RAG.
Implement citation validation and faithfulness checking.
Defend against prompt injection and document poisoning attacks.
searchText: Grounding & Safety Ensure answers are faithful to sources and defend against abuse. grounding-safety safety grounding citations prompt-injection Explain the difference between hallucination and fabrication in RAG. Implement citation validation and faithfulness checking. Defend against prompt injection and document poisoning attacks. Goals - Understand RAG-specific failure modes: hallucination vs. fabrication. - Learn techniques to verify answer grounding. - Implement defenses against prompt injection and document poisoning. Prereqs - Read: **Context Shaping** (grounding depends on good context). - Challenge: **Basic Retrieval** (you need a working pipeline to test). Core idea Hallucination in RAG Even with perfect retrieval, LLMs can: - **Fabricate facts** not in any source. - **Misattribute claims** to the wrong source. - **Over-generalize** from limited evidence. RAG reduces but doesn't eliminate hallucination. You need verification. Grounding techniques **1. Citation Validation** Check that each citation actually supports the claim: **2. Faithfulness Checking** Verify the entire answer is derivable from context: **3. Self-RAG Pattern** Add reflection tokens during generation: - [Retrieval Needed?] → decide if more context is needed - [Relevant?] → verify retrieved chunks are relevant - [Supported?] → check if generation is supported Security threats **Prompt Injection** User input contains instructions that hijack the LLM: Defense: - Sanitize user input (remove instruction-like patterns). - Use separate system/user channels. - Add guardrails that detect jailbreak attempts. **Document Poisoning** Malicious content in indexed documents: Defense: - Validate document sources before indexing. - Use access controls (users only see docs they're allowed to). - Add content filtering during ingestion. **Indirect Prompt Injection** Instructions hidden in retrieved documents: Defense: - Treat all retrieved content as untrusted user input. - Use instruction hierarchy (system > user > retrieved). - Detect and flag instruction-like patterns in documents. Failure modes - **False positives**: valid answers flagged as unsupported. - **Overly strict**: requiring exact quotes blocks paraphrasing. - **Missing attacks**: sanitization doesn't catch all injection variants. - **Performance overhead**: verification adds latency. Production defaults - Always require citations in system prompt. - Run faithfulness check on high-stakes queries. - Sanitize user input before embedding or prompting. - Use instruction hierarchy: system prompt is authoritative. - Log all queries and answers for audit. title: Query Transforms
description: Turn vague user queries into precise retrieval instructions.
outcomes: Explain why raw user queries often fail to retrieve the right chunks.
Implement three query transformation techniques: rewriting, expansion, and HyDE.
Know when query transforms help vs. when they add latency without benefit.
searchText: Query Transforms Turn vague user queries into precise retrieval instructions. pre-retrieval retrieval query-transforms hyde rewriting Explain why raw user queries often fail to retrieve the right chunks. Implement three query transformation techniques: rewriting, expansion, and HyDE. Know when query transforms help vs. when they add latency without benefit. Goals - Understand the "query-document mismatch" problem. - Learn three techniques to bridge this gap. - Know when to skip query transforms (simplicity vs. latency tradeoff). Prereqs - Read: **Your First RAG** (you need a working retrieval pipeline first). - Challenge: **Basic Retrieval** (to see the problem firsthand). Core idea The mismatch problem Users ask questions in natural language: > "How do I make my RAG faster?" But documents are written in technical prose: > "Optimize retrieval latency by implementing semantic caching..." The embedding of the question and the embedding of the answer may not be close enough in vector space. This is the **query-document mismatch**. Three transformation techniques **1. Query Rewriting** Use an LLM to rephrase the query into search-optimized form: - "make RAG faster" → "RAG latency optimization techniques" - Removes filler words, expands acronyms, adds synonyms **2. Query Expansion (Multi-Query)** Generate multiple query variants and union the results: - Original + 2-3 rewrites → retrieve from all → dedupe + rerank **3. HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embedding)** Generate a hypothetical answer, then search for chunks similar to it: - Query: "What is chunking?" - Hypothetical answer: "Chunking is the process of splitting documents..." - Embed the answer, retrieve chunks similar to it When to use each | Technique | Latency | When it helps | |-----------|---------|---------------| | Rewrite | +100-300ms | Vague queries, typos, colloquial language | | Multi-Query | +200-500ms | Recall is more important than latency | | HyDE | +300-800ms | Technical domains where query ≠ doc style | Failure modes - **Over-transformation**: LLM rewrites change the meaning of the query. - **Latency explosion**: chaining transforms adds 1-2s before retrieval. - **Hallucination in HyDE**: hypothetical answer leads to wrong retrievals. - **Unnecessary complexity**: simple keyword queries may work just as well. Production defaults - Start without transforms. Measure retrieval quality first. - Add rewriting only if you see user queries consistently failing. - Use HyDE for technical/scientific domains where it's proven to help. - Always A/B test: transforms can hurt as much as help. title: How Much Data Do You Need for RAG?
description: Understanding data requirements for RAG systems - from 10 pages to millions of documents.
outcomes: Understand that RAG works with ANY amount of data.
Know when to use RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context.
Size your RAG system appropriately for your use case.
searchText: How Much Data Do You Need for RAG? Understanding data requirements for RAG systems - from 10 pages to millions of documents. foundations foundations data sizing architecture Understand that RAG works with ANY amount of data. Know when to use RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context. Size your RAG system appropriately for your use case. Goals - Understand that RAG works with any amount of data (10 pages to millions of documents) - Learn when to use RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context windows - Know how to size your RAG system for your specific use case Prereqs - Basic understanding of what RAG is (retrieval + generation) - Familiarity with embeddings and vector search concepts Core idea **RAG works with ANY amount of data** — from 10 pages to 10 million documents. The question isn't "how much data do I need?" but rather: - **What problem am I solving?** - **How specific is my domain?** - **What's my latency/cost budget?** You can absolutely build a useful RAG system with 10 pages. In fact, many production RAG systems work best with focused, high-quality data rather than massive datasets. The data size spectrum 10-100 Pages (Small) **Use cases**: Personal knowledge base, internal FAQ, single-product documentation **Examples**: - Company handbook → HR chatbot - API documentation → Developer assistant - Course syllabus → Student Q&A **Why it works**: - Dense, specific information - High relevance per chunk - Fast retrieval (milliseconds) - Low infrastructure cost **Reality check**: Many successful RAG products started here! 100-10,000 Pages (Medium) **Use cases**: Enterprise docs, multi-product support, research papers **Examples**: - All Stripe documentation - Academic paper collection - Legal contract library **Considerations**: - Chunking strategy matters more - May need reranking for precision - Hybrid search (semantic + keyword) helps 10,000+ Pages (Large) **Use cases**: Enterprise search, legal discovery, code repositories **Examples**: - Wikipedia-scale knowledge - GitHub codebase search - Multi-tenant SaaS with isolated data **Considerations**: - Vector DB selection crucial - Metadata filtering essential - Cost optimization (caching, tiered retrieval) When RAG beats alternatives RAG vs Long Context Windows | Criteria | RAG | Long Context (100K+ tokens) | | ------------------ | ------------------------- | --------------------------- | | **Cost** | $0.001-0.01/query | $0.10-1.00/query | | **Latency** | ~100-500ms | ~2-10 seconds | | **Data freshness** | Real-time updates | Requires new prompt | | **Scalability** | Billions of docs | Limited by context | | **Precision** | High (targeted retrieval) | "Lost in the middle" risk | **Rule of thumb**: If your data fits in 50K tokens AND rarely changes → consider long context. Otherwise → RAG. RAG vs Fine-tuning | Criteria | RAG | Fine-tuning | | --------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------- | | **Setup time** | Hours | Days-weeks | | **Data updates** | Instant | Requires retraining | | **Factual accuracy** | Grounded in sources | Can hallucinate | | **Cost** | Per-query retrieval | Upfront training | | **Citability** | Built-in sources | No sources | | **Style control** | Limited | Excellent | | **Domain vocabulary** | Good with hybrid search | Trained into model | **Key insight from vinija.ai**: - **RAG excels at**: Factual, access-controlled, timely information. Real-time updates without retraining. Scalable with flexible external sources. - **Fine-tuning excels at**: Adapting style, tone, and vocabulary. Your linguistic "paint brush" for the desired domain. - **Best practice**: Focus on RAG first for connecting specialized data. Once functional, add fine-tuning to enhance style and vocabulary if needed. **Rule of thumb**: If you need citations or frequent updates → RAG. If you need behavior/style changes → fine-tune. For production excellence → consider both. Failure modes Even with 10 pages, RAG can fail: 1. Chunk size mismatch **Problem**: Default 512-token chunks are too big for your 10-page FAQ. **Fix**: Try 128-256 token chunks, or sentence-level for very short docs. 2. Over-retrieval **Problem**: Top-10 retrieval includes irrelevant chunks from your 20 total chunks. **Fix**: Use top-3 or add reranking, even on small datasets. 3. Sparse queries **Problem**: User asks "how do I X?" but your docs say "to X, you should..." **Fix**: Query expansion or HyDE to bridge vocabulary gap. Production defaults For 10-100 pages: For 100-10K pages: For 10K+ pages: Real examples of small-data RAG 1. **Notion AI** — Works on your personal workspace (often Start small. A 10-page RAG system that solves a real problem is infinitely more valuable than a million-doc system that nobody uses.

title: RAG vs Long Context Windows
description: When to use retrieval vs stuffing everything into a massive context window.
outcomes: Compare cost, latency, and accuracy of RAG vs long context
Understand the 'Lost in the Middle' phenomenon
Make informed architectural decisions for your use case
searchText: RAG vs Long Context Windows When to use retrieval vs stuffing everything into a massive context window. foundations architecture context-windows cost trade-offs Compare cost, latency, and accuracy of RAG vs long context Understand the 'Lost in the Middle' phenomenon Make informed architectural decisions for your use case Goals - Understand when RAG beats long context windows (and vice versa). - Calculate real-world costs of each approach. - Know the "Lost in the Middle" failure mode. Prereqs - **Tokenizers and Context** (Phase 0). - **Why RAG Exists** (Phase 0). Core idea With models like Gemini 1.5 Pro (2M tokens) and Claude 3.5 (200K tokens), a natural question arises: > **"Why bother with RAG? Just stuff everything into the context!"** This lesson explains why that's often a bad idea. The Naive Approach: "Just Use More Context" This works! But at what cost? --- The Hidden Costs of Long Context 1. Computational Cost Processing extremely long contexts requires massive hardware resources. | Context Length | Hardware Required | Estimated Cost/Hour | | -------------- | ----------------- | ------------------- | | 128K tokens | 1-2 H100 GPUs | $5-10 | | 1M tokens | 8-16 H100 GPUs | $50-80 | | 10M tokens | 32+ H100 GPUs | **$100+** | The KV-cache alone for a 10M token context can exceed **1 terabyte of VRAM**. 2. Latency and Throughput As context length increases, inference time grows significantly: 3. The "Lost in the Middle" Problem This is the critical failure mode that makes long context unreliable. **Key finding from Liu et al., 2023:** > LLMs are significantly better at using information at the **beginning** and **end** of the context. Information in the **middle** is often ignored. **Practical implication:** If your critical information happens to land in the middle of a 1M token context, the model may simply not use it—even though it's right there! --- RAG: A Targeted, Cost-Efficient Solution RAG addresses all three problems: | Problem | Long Context | RAG | | ---------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | **Compute Cost** | $100+/hour for 10M tokens | $0.01-0.10 per query | | **Latency** | Seconds to minutes | Milliseconds retrieval + normal LLM | | **Middle Loss** | Information gets buried | Only relevant chunks in context | | **Freshness** | Requires re-ingesting everything | Update individual documents | How RAG Stays Efficient --- When to Use Each Approach Use Long Context When: - ✅ You have a **single document** that must be processed entirely (legal contract analysis) - ✅ You need **cross-document reasoning** over a small set of docs - ✅ **Latency isn't critical** and **cost is not a concern** - ✅ The task requires **seeing everything at once** (comprehensive summarization) Use RAG When: - ✅ You have a **large corpus** (thousands of documents) - ✅ Questions are **specific** (looking for particular facts) - ✅ **Cost and latency matter** (production systems) - ✅ Knowledge needs **frequent updates** - ✅ You need **citations** (RAG can point to source documents) The Best of Both: Hierarchical RAG For complex tasks, combine both approaches: --- Production defaults | Scenario | Recommended Approach | | ----------------------- | -------------------------------- | | Customer support bot | RAG (fast, cheap, updatable) | | Legal document analysis | Long context (need full doc) | | Research assistant | RAG + long context for synthesis | | Real-time chat | RAG (latency critical) | | Summarize single report | Long context | | Search across 10K docs | RAG (only option that scales) | **Start with RAG.** Only use long context when you genuinely need the model to see everything at once. In most production scenarios, RAG wins on cost, latency, and reliability. --- Failure modes ❌ Assuming Long Context is "Smarter" More context ≠ better answers. Middle-loss means the model might miss critical info. ❌ Ignoring Cost at Scale What costs $1 in prototyping can cost $10,000/month in production with long context. ❌ Not Testing Position Sensitivity If using long context, test what happens when key info is in different positions. --- Do next - Query Transforms - Improve retrieval quality - RAG Data Sizing - Right-size your RAG system

title: Auto-Merging Retrieval
description: Hierarchical retrieval that automatically merges fragmented chunks into coherent context.
outcomes: Understand the fragmentation problem with small chunks
Implement auto-merging retrieval for coherent context
Choose between sentence-window and auto-merging strategies
searchText: Auto-Merging Retrieval Hierarchical retrieval that automatically merges fragmented chunks into coherent context. production-ops retrieval auto-merge hierarchical chunking Understand the fragmentation problem with small chunks Implement auto-merging retrieval for coherent context Choose between sentence-window and auto-merging strategies Goals - Understand why naive small-chunk retrieval causes fragmentation. - Learn the auto-merging algorithm for coherent context. - Choose the right retrieval strategy for your use case. Prereqs - **Sentence-Window Retrieval** (Phase 2). - **Chunking Mastery** (Phase 2). Core idea The Problem: Chunk Fragmentation When you use small chunks for precise retrieval, you often get **fragmented results**: **The problem gets worse with smaller chunks** — you get more precise matches but more fragmented context. The Solution: Auto-Merging Retrieval Auto-merging retrieval builds a **hierarchical index** and automatically merges child chunks back into their parent when enough children are retrieved. --- The Auto-Merging Algorithm Step 1: Build Hierarchical Index Create a tree structure where leaves are small chunks and parents are larger segments. Step 2: Index Leaf Nodes Only Only embed and index the smallest (leaf) chunks for retrieval. Step 3: Retrieve and Auto-Merge The key algorithm: if enough children of a parent are retrieved, replace them with the parent. --- Sentence-Window vs Auto-Merging | Aspect | Sentence-Window | Auto-Merging | | --------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | **Context expansion** | Fixed window around match | Dynamic based on retrieved siblings | | **Index structure** | Flat (with metadata) | Hierarchical tree | | **Best for** | Uniform documents | Documents with natural structure | | **Implementation** | Simpler | More complex | | **Context coherence** | Window may cross topics | Respects document structure | When to Use Each **Use Sentence-Window when:** - Documents have uniform structure (news articles, chat logs) - You want simpler implementation - Fixed context windows work well **Use Auto-Merging when:** - Documents have natural hierarchy (textbooks, legal docs, technical manuals) - Queries often span related subsections - You need the context to respect document structure --- LlamaIndex Implementation --- Failure modes ❌ Wrong Hierarchy Levels If chunk sizes don't match document structure, merging produces incoherent context. - **Fix**: Analyze your documents to determine natural boundaries (sections, paragraphs). ❌ Merge Threshold Too Low Setting threshold too low (e.g., 0.2) causes over-merging, returning huge contexts. - **Fix**: Start with 0.5 and tune based on evaluation. ❌ Merge Threshold Too High Setting threshold too high (e.g., 0.9) rarely triggers merging. - **Fix**: If you're seeing fragmented results, lower the threshold. ❌ Ignoring Document Structure Using auto-merging on unstructured documents (chat logs, random notes) adds complexity without benefit. - **Fix**: Use sentence-window for unstructured content. --- Production defaults | Setting | Recommended Value | | -------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | **Hierarchy levels** | 3 (section → paragraph → sentence) | | **Chunk sizes** | [2048, 512, 128] tokens | | **Merge threshold** | 0.5 (50% of siblings) | | **Initial top-k** | 10-15 leaf nodes | | **Embedding model** | Same for all levels | --- Do next - Reranking Strategies - Improve result quality after retrieval - RAPTOR Retrieval - Tree-structured summarization approach

title: Caching Strategies
description: Reduce latency and cost with smart caching at every layer.
outcomes: Implement embedding, retrieval, and semantic caches.
Design cache invalidation strategies.
Know when caching helps vs hurts.
searchText: Caching Strategies Reduce latency and cost with smart caching at every layer. production-ops caching performance latency cost Implement embedding, retrieval, and semantic caches. Design cache invalidation strategies. Know when caching helps vs hurts. Goals - Understand caching opportunities in RAG pipelines. - Implement safe caching with proper invalidation. - Balance cache hit rate vs freshness. Prereqs - Read: **Metadata Filtering** (understand retrieval flow). Core idea Where to cache in RAG Cache types and their tradeoffs | Cache Type | Hit Rate | Invalidation | Risk | |------------|----------|--------------|------| | **Embedding** | High | Never (deterministic) | None | | **Retrieval** | Medium | On index update | Stale results | | **Semantic** | Low-Medium | Complex | Wrong answers | 1. Embedding cache (SAFE) Embeddings are deterministic—same input always produces same output: Embedding caching is free performance. Always do it. No invalidation needed unless you change models. 2. Retrieval results cache (CAREFUL) Cache search results, but invalidate on index updates: 3. Semantic response cache (RISKY) Cache full answers for repeated questions: Semantic caching can return stale or wrong answers. Use high thresholds (0.95+) and short TTLs. 4. LLM prompt caching (PROVIDER-SPECIFIC) Some providers cache large prompts server-side: Cache invalidation strategies | Strategy | When to Use | Complexity | |----------|-------------|------------| | **TTL-based** | Time-insensitive data | Low | | **Version-based** | Index updates | Medium | | **Event-driven** | Document changes | High | | **Hybrid** | Production systems | High | Failure modes 1. **No invalidation**: Serving stale results forever. 2. **Over-caching**: Semantic cache with low threshold → wrong answers. 3. **Cache stampede**: Many requests hit expired cache simultaneously. 4. **Memory bloat**: Unbounded cache growth. Production defaults - **Embedding cache**: Always enable, 30-day TTL. - **Retrieval cache**: Enable with version-based invalidation, 1-hour TTL. - **Semantic cache**: Disable by default; enable only for stable, high-volume queries. - **Prompt caching**: Enable if provider supports it. Implement structure-aware chunking for complex documents. Debug chunking failures and measure their impact on retrieval. Goals - Build a mental model for choosing chunking strategies. - Master advanced techniques: semantic, hierarchical, and contextual chunking. - Know how to measure chunking quality. Prereqs - Read: **Chunking 101** (basic concepts). - Challenge: `simple-chunking` (implement fixed-size chunks). Core idea Why chunking matters Chunking is **the most underrated** part of RAG: - Bad chunks → wrong retrieval → wrong answers - Chunks are the **unit of retrieval**—you can't retrieve information if it's split across chunks - Chunk boundaries determine what context the LLM sees The chunking decision tree Chunking strategies compared | Strategy | Chunk Size | Best For | Complexity | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------- | ---------- | | **Fixed-size** | 200-500 tokens | Simple baseline | Low | | **Recursive** | 300-600 tokens | General purpose | Low | | **Sentence** | 1-3 sentences | High precision needs | Low | | **Markdown/HTML** | Varies | Structured docs | Medium | | **Code-aware** | Functions/classes | Code repositories | Medium | | **Semantic** | Varies | Topic boundaries | High | | **Sentence-window** | Small retrieve, large context | Precise + context | Medium | | **Parent-document** | Small child, large parent | Multi-level needs | Medium | | **Hierarchical (RAPTOR)** | Multi-level summaries | Very long docs | High | | **Contextual** | + prepended context | Any (enhancement) | Medium | Strategy deep dives 1. Recursive chunking (default) Split by paragraphs, then sentences, then characters to hit target size: 2. Structure-aware chunking For Markdown, respect headers: 3. Sentence-window chunking Retrieve small, expand to larger context: 4. Contextual chunking (Anthropic's approach) Prepend document/section context to each chunk: Contextual retrieval (adding document context to chunks) improved retrieval by 49% in their tests. It's a simple enhancement to any chunking strategy. 5. Hierarchical chunking (RAPTOR) Create multi-level summaries: 6. Semantic chunking Split text based on meaning rather than syntax. Measure cosine similarity between adjacent sentences; if similarity drops below a threshold, start a new chunk. **Pros**: Highly coherent chunks. **Cons**: Requires embedding model inference (slower), sensitive to threshold. Failure modes 1. **Chunks too small**: Lose context, retrieve fragments. 2. **Chunks too large**: Dilute relevance, waste tokens. 3. **Splitting mid-thought**: Tables, lists, code blocks broken. 4. **No overlap**: Miss information at boundaries. 5. **Ignoring structure**: Treating Markdown as plain text. 6. **Not measuring**: Can't improve what you don't measure. Production defaults - **Default**: Recursive chunking, 300-600 tokens, 10-20% overlap. - **Structured docs**: Markdown/HTML-aware chunking. - **Code**: AST-based chunking (tree-sitter). - **Enhancement**: Add contextual headers to all chunks. - **Long docs**: Consider parent-document or RAPTOR. Measuring chunking quality Do next See chunking in the encyclopedia: Playbook: RAG Techniques Encyclopedia →

searchText: Context Window Optimization Combat lost-in-the-middle with compression, ordering, and budgeting. post-retrieval context-window compression lost-in-middle ordering Understand and mitigate the lost-in-the-middle effect. Implement context compression and intelligent ordering. Set and enforce token budgets. Goals - Understand why context placement affects answer quality. - Master compression techniques to fit more signal in less space. - Build reliable token budget enforcement. Prereqs - Read: **Query Transform Patterns** (you have good retrieval results). - Read: **Tokenizers & Context Windows** (understand token limits). Core idea The lost-in-the-middle problem From Liu et al., 2023: LLMs are **not equally good** at using information from all parts of the context. **Key finding**: Information in the middle of the context is often ignored. Put important content at the beginning and end. Context window budget You have limited tokens. Use them wisely: Mitigation strategies 1. Smart ordering Put best evidence first and last: 2. Extractive compression Keep only relevant sentences: 3. LLM-based compression Use an LLM to summarize while preserving key info: LLM compression can introduce errors. Use extractive compression for high-stakes applications. 4. Token budget enforcement Never exceed your budget: Advanced: Selective augmentation From RECOMP: Sometimes adding context **hurts**. Only augment when it helps: Failure modes 1. **Stuffing everything**: More context ≠ better answers. 2. **Ignoring ordering**: Putting best evidence in the middle. 3. **No budget enforcement**: Exceeding context limits → truncation by the model. 4. **Over-compression**: Losing critical information. 5. **Compression hallucinations**: LLM-based compression adding false info. Production defaults - **Ordering**: Best evidence first, second-best last. - **Compression**: Extractive first, LLM-based only if needed. - **Budget**: Reserve 30% for response generation. - **Chunks**: 5-10 chunks after reranking. Implement model routing for cost-quality tradeoffs. Build cost monitoring and alerting. Goals - Understand where costs come from in RAG. - Implement strategies to reduce costs 50-80%. - Build cost monitoring that prevents surprises. Prereqs - Read: **Caching Strategies** (first line of cost defense). Core idea RAG cost breakdown Typical cost distribution: **Key insight**: LLM generation dominates. Optimize there first. Cost drivers | Component | Cost Per | Optimization Lever | |-----------|----------|-------------------| | **LLM (input)** | 1M tokens | Compression, shorter prompts | | **LLM (output)** | 1M tokens | Shorter responses, streaming | | **Embeddings** | 1M tokens | Caching, batch processing | | **Reranking** | Per call | Cascade, skip when possible | | **Vector DB** | Storage + queries | Index optimization | Strategy 1: Model routing Use expensive models only when needed: Strategy 2: Context compression Reduce input tokens: Strategy 3: Batch embedding Batch requests to reduce overhead: Strategy 4: Skip reranking when confident Cost monitoring Track costs in real-time: Cost reduction checklist 1. **Embedding cache**: 50-80% reduction in embedding costs 2. **Model routing**: 40-60% reduction in LLM costs 3. **Context compression**: 20-40% reduction in input tokens 4. **Batch processing**: 10-20% reduction in API overhead 5. **Skip reranking**: 30-50% reduction in reranking costs Failure modes 1. **Over-optimizing**: Quality drops noticeably. 2. **No monitoring**: Surprise bills. 3. **Wrong routing**: Expensive model for simple queries. 4. **Stale caches**: Wrong answers to save money. title: Hybrid Retrieval Deep Dive
description: Master BM25 + Dense fusion for production-grade recall.
outcomes: Explain when sparse beats dense and vice versa.
Implement RRF fusion with proper k parameter tuning.
Debug retrieval failures using hybrid diagnostics.
searchText: Hybrid Retrieval Deep Dive Master BM25 + Dense fusion for production-grade recall. retrieval hybrid retrieval bm25 rrf fusion Explain when sparse beats dense and vice versa. Implement RRF fusion with proper k parameter tuning. Debug retrieval failures using hybrid diagnostics. Goals - Understand WHY hybrid retrieval beats single-mode in most production systems. - Master the RRF formula and its k parameter. - Know when to weight sparse vs dense differently. Prereqs - Read: **Query Transforms** (you should have basic retrieval working). - Challenge: `bm25-from-scratch` (implement BM25 scoring). Core idea The fundamental tradeoff | Query Type | BM25 Wins | Dense Wins | |------------|-----------|------------| | "AWS error code E-3847" | ✓ Exact match | ✗ Semantic noise | | "how to make api faster" | ✗ Vocabulary mismatch | ✓ Semantic similarity | | "python timeout exception" | Tie | Tie | **Key insight**: Production queries are a MIX. You need BOTH. Why not just use one? **Dense-only problems:** - Misses exact matches (IDs, codes, proper nouns) - Embeddings can cluster unrelated terms - "AWS-3847" might retrieve "GCP-1234" because they're both cloud errors **BM25-only problems:** - Misses paraphrases ("renew secrets" vs "rotate API keys") - No semantic understanding - Vocabulary mismatch kills recall Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) The industry-standard fusion algorithm from Cormack et al., 2009: Why k=60? From the original paper: - **k=60** was empirically found to be robust across datasets - **Lower k (e.g., 10)**: Top ranks dominate heavily - **Higher k (e.g., 100)**: Flatter distribution, more "averaging" k=60 is a solid default. Only tune if you have labeled data showing different k improves your specific retrieval task. When to weight sparse vs dense differently | Corpus Type | Recommended Weighting | |-------------|----------------------| | Technical docs (IDs, codes) | BM25 weight: 1.5x | | Conversational content | Dense weight: 1.5x | | Mixed/unknown | Equal (RRF default) | Failure modes 1. **Dense-only blindness**: Miss exact matches for IDs, codes, proper nouns. 2. **BM25-only blindness**: Miss paraphrases, synonyms, semantic matches. 3. **Wrong k value**: Rarely matters, but can hurt on extreme datasets. 4. **Not normalizing BM25 scores**: If using score-based fusion (not rank-based), BM25 scores vary wildly by query. 5. **Misaligned indexes**: BM25 index and vector index must cover the same documents. Production defaults - **Use RRF** (rank-based) over score-based fusion—more robust. - **k=60** unless you have data showing otherwise. - **Retrieve 50-100 from each source**, fuse, then rerank top-20/50. - **Log both sources**: Know which retriever contributed winning docs. title: Late Chunking for Context-Aware Embeddings
description: Preserve cross-chunk context by embedding documents before chunking.
outcomes: Understand the context loss problem in naive chunking.
Implement late chunking with long-context embedding models.
Compare late chunking vs early chunking retrieval quality.
searchText: Late Chunking for Context-Aware Embeddings Preserve cross-chunk context by embedding documents before chunking. retrieval chunking embeddings context-preservation jina-ai Understand the context loss problem in naive chunking. Implement late chunking with long-context embedding models. Compare late chunking vs early chunking retrieval quality. import { Callout } from "@/components/ui/Callout"; import { Card } from "@/components/ui/Card"; import Link from "next/link"; Goals - Understand why naive chunking loses important context. - Learn the late chunking technique pioneered by Jina AI. - Implement late chunking with long-context models. Prereqs Before this lesson, ensure you understand: - Basic chunking strategies (fixed-size, sentence-based) - How embeddings represent semantic meaning - Token-level vs sentence-level embeddings Core idea Traditional chunking pipelines follow this order: **Chunk → Embed**. This causes context loss because each chunk is embedded independently without access to surrounding context. Late chunking **inverts the order**: **Embed → Chunk** 1. **Embed the entire document** using a long-context model (8K+ tokens) 2. **Get token-level embeddings** (before the final pooling layer) 3. **Apply chunking boundaries** to the token sequence 4. **Mean-pool each chunk's tokens** to get chunk embeddings The magic: each token's embedding already "sees" the full document context through the transformer's attention mechanism. The Pronoun Problem When Chunk 2 is embedded independently, "She" has no referent—the model doesn't know it refers to Alice. Implementation Failure modes **Model context limits**: If your document exceeds 8192 tokens, you must split first, losing some cross-section context. **Compute cost**: Late chunking requires running the full document through the model, which is more expensive than embedding smaller chunks. **Token-to-character mapping**: Off-by-one errors in mapping token indices to character boundaries cause misaligned chunks. **Memory pressure**: Long documents with 8K tokens require substantial GPU memory for the full attention matrix. Production defaults | Setting | Recommended Value | Notes | | -------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | Model | `jina-embeddings-v2-base-en` | 8K context, designed for late chunking | | Chunk size | 300-500 chars | Balance retrieval precision vs context | | Overlap | 50-100 chars | Maintains some boundary context | | Max doc length | 8000 tokens | Leave headroom below model limit | **When to use late chunking:** - Narrative documents (stories, transcripts, conversations) - Documents with many pronouns and coreferences - Legal/medical documents where context is critical **When to skip:** - Factual, self-contained content (FAQs, definitions) - Speed-critical applications - Short documents under 1000 tokens Do next Learn about late interaction: ColBERT and Late Interaction →

searchText: Metadata Filtering & Routing Use metadata to reduce search space and route queries intelligently. retrieval metadata filtering routing performance Design effective metadata schemas for filtering. Implement filter-first retrieval for performance. Build query routers that pick the right index/strategy. Goals - Design metadata schemas that enable efficient filtering. - Understand filter-first vs filter-after tradeoffs. - Build intelligent query routers. Prereqs - Read: **Context Window Optimization** (you understand retrieval flow). Core idea Why metadata filtering matters Without filtering, every query searches your **entire corpus**. With filtering: - **Faster**: Search smaller subset - **More relevant**: Exclude irrelevant documents - **Multi-tenant safe**: Enforce access control Metadata schema design Filter-first vs filter-after | Approach | Speed | Recall | Use When | |----------|-------|--------|----------| | **Filter-first** | Fast | Lower | User specifies clear scope | | **Filter-after** | Slow | Higher | Unsure what user wants | | **Hybrid** | Medium | High | Production default | Self-query: LLM extracts filters Let the LLM parse natural language into structured filters: Query routing Route different queries to different retrieval strategies: Multi-index routing Different indexes for different content: Failure modes 1. **No tenant isolation**: Security vulnerability. 2. **Over-filtering**: Miss relevant results. 3. **Under-filtering**: Search too much, slow + noisy. 4. **Stale metadata**: Filters based on outdated info. 5. **Filter explosion**: Too many filter dimensions. Production defaults - **Always filter by tenant** (non-negotiable for multi-tenant). - **Log filter usage** for debugging and optimization. - **Self-query for complex queries** only (adds latency). - **Index per content type** if content is heterogeneous. searchText: Query Transformation Patterns Boost recall with HyDE, multi-query, step-back, and decomposition. query-transforms query-transforms hyde multi-query step-back Implement 4+ query transformation techniques. Know when each technique helps vs hurts. Build a query transformation router. Goals - Master the 4 main query transformation patterns. - Build intuition for when to use each. - Implement a router that picks the right technique. Prereqs - Read: **Query Transforms** (basic concepts from Phase 1). - Challenge: `hyde-search` (implement HyDE). Core idea The query-document mismatch problem Users write **queries**. Your corpus has **documents**. They speak different languages: | Query | What the document says | |-------|------------------------| | "make it faster" | "Performance optimization: implement caching..." | | "renew secrets" | "API key rotation policy: rotate every 90 days..." | | "what went wrong" | "Error handling: NullPointerException occurs when..." | Query transforms bridge this gap. The 4 main patterns 1. HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) From Gao et al., 2022: **When HyDE helps:** - Short queries (1-3 words) - Vague queries ("make it better") - Domain vocabulary mismatch **When to skip:** - Already specific queries - Keyword searches (use BM25) - Latency-critical paths (adds 200-500ms) 2. Multi-query generation Generate query variations to improve recall: 3. Step-back prompting From Zheng et al., 2023: **Example:** - Specific: "Why did my Python 3.9 async code fail on AWS Lambda?" - Step-back: "What are the limitations of async in AWS Lambda?" 4. Query decomposition For multi-hop questions: **Example:** - Original: "How does Company A's RAG system compare to Company B's?" - Sub-questions: 1. "What is Company A's RAG architecture?" 2. "What is Company B's RAG architecture?" 3. "What metrics should be used to compare RAG systems?" Query transformation router Not every query needs transformation. Build a router: Failure modes 1. **Over-transformation**: Adding latency for simple queries. 2. **HyDE hallucinations**: The hypothetical may be wrong (but often still helps!). 3. **Too many sub-queries**: Decomposition can explode complexity. 4. **Ignoring original query**: Always include original alongside transforms. Production defaults - **Default**: No transformation (direct retrieval). - **Short/vague queries**: HyDE. - **Multi-hop**: Decomposition. - **Always**: Log which transform was used for debugging. searchText: Reranking Strategies Boost precision with cross-encoders, ColBERT, and LLM rerankers. post-retrieval reranking cross-encoder colbert precision monobert duobert Explain the difference between bi-encoders and cross-encoders. Know when to use cross-encoder vs ColBERT vs LLM reranking. Implement a reranking cascade for latency-quality tradeoffs. Goals - Understand why reranking is the "precision lever" in RAG. - Master the tradeoffs between different reranking approaches. - Know when reranking is worth the latency cost. Prereqs - Read: **Hybrid Retrieval** (you need candidates before you can rerank). - Challenge: `reranker-score-function` (implement basic scoring). Core idea The retrieval-rerank pattern Retrieval optimizes for **recall** (don't miss anything). Reranking optimizes for **precision** (put the best at the top). Why reranking matters From the Lost in the Middle paper: LLMs struggle when relevant information is buried in the context. Reranking ensures the **best evidence is at the top**. Bi-encoder vs Cross-encoder | Aspect | Bi-encoder (Retrieval) | Cross-encoder (Rerank) | | ---------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------- | | **How it works** | Encode query and docs separately | Encode query+doc together | | **Speed** | Fast (precompute doc embeddings) | Slow (N forward passes) | | **Accuracy** | Good recall | Better precision | | **Use case** | First-stage retrieval | Second-stage reranking | **Cross-encoder** sees the query and document together, allowing fine-grained attention: Reranking methods compared | Method | Quality | Latency | Cost | Best For | | ----------------- | --------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- | | **Cross-encoder** | High | +100-300ms | Medium | Default production choice | | **ColBERT** | High | +50-150ms | Infra-heavy | Large corpora, speed-critical | | **LLM rerank** | Very high | +500-2000ms | High | Hard queries, low volume | | **Cascade** | Tunable | Tunable | Tunable | Latency-sensitive systems | Cross-encoder reranking The most common production pattern: Neural Reranker Paradigms: Pointwise, Pairwise, Listwise Neural rerankers are classified into three methodological paradigms based on how they evaluate relevance: | Paradigm | Model Examples | How It Works | Tradeoffs | | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | | **Pointwise** | monoBERT | Score each query-doc pair independently | High quality, slow (N forward passes) | | **Pairwise** | duoBERT | Compare pairs of documents: "Is A more relevant than B?" | Better fine-grained distinctions | | **Listwise** | ListBERT, ListT5 | Consider full list of documents together | Best for zero-shot, state-of-the-art | **monoBERT** (Pointwise): Each document is scored independently. Concatenate query and doc with [SEP], predict relevance score. **duoBERT** (Pairwise): Extends monoBERT by comparing pairs - "Given query Q, is document A more relevant than B?" Typically used as a second stage after monoBERT to resolve fine-grained distinctions. **ListBERT/ListT5** (Listwise): Consider the full list of documents simultaneously using listwise loss functions (ListMLE, Softmax Cross Entropy). ListT5 uses Fusion-in-Decoder architecture and achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot retrieval. ColBERT: Late Interaction for Fine-Grained Matching ColBERT (Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT) offers a compelling middle ground between bi-encoders and cross-encoders. The Late Interaction Paradigm Unlike cross-encoders that process query+doc together, ColBERT uses **late interaction**: MaxSim: The Scoring Mechanism MaxSim computes the maximum similarity between each query token and ALL document tokens: $$\text{Score}(q, d) = \sum_{i=1}^{|q|} \max_{j=1}^{|d|} \cos(q_i, d_j)$$ Why MaxSim Works Consider query "sweet apple" and two documents: - **Doc 1**: "The apple is sweet and crisp" → High MaxSim (both tokens match) - **Doc 2**: "The banana is yellow" → Low MaxSim (neither token matches well) This **token-level matching** captures fine-grained relevance that bi-encoders miss. ColBERT vs Cross-Encoder Trade-offs | Aspect | Cross-Encoder | ColBERT | | ------------------ | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | **Accuracy** | Slightly higher | Very close | | **Latency** | ~100-300ms/query | ~50-100ms/query | | **Precomputation** | None (recompute each time) | Doc embeddings precomputed | | **Storage** | Minimal | Heavy (all token embeddings) | Storage Considerations ColBERT's main drawback is storage. For each document: - Standard embedding: 1 vector (768 dims × 4 bytes = 3KB) - ColBERT: ~128 vectors (128 tokens × 128 dims × 4 bytes = **64KB per doc**) For 100,000 documents: **~6.4 GB** just for ColBERT embeddings. When to Use ColBERT ✅ **Good fit:** - Large corpus with speed requirements - Queries benefit from fine-grained token matching - You have storage budget for token embeddings ❌ **Not ideal:** - Storage is constrained - Simple queries (bi-encoder sufficient) - Very few documents (cross-encoder is fast enough) ColBERT v2 and ColPali **ColBERTv2**: Adds compression to reduce storage by 6-10x while maintaining quality. **ColPali**: Extends late interaction to **multimodal retrieval**, processing PDF screenshots directly instead of OCR text. LLM reranking (listwise) For the hardest queries, use an LLM to reason about relevance: LLM reranking is expensive and slow. Use only when: (1) queries are hard, (2) volume is low, (3) stakes are high. Reranking cascade For latency-sensitive systems, use a cascade: Failure modes 1. **Reranking too few candidates**: Rerank at least 20-50. If you only rerank top-5, you might miss the best result. 2. **Reranking too many**: Diminishing returns + latency. 50-100 is usually enough. 3. **Model mismatch**: Use rerankers trained on similar domains (MS MARCO for general, domain-specific for specialized). 4. **Ignoring diversity**: Reranking by relevance alone can create redundant results. Consider MMR. Production defaults - **Default**: Cross-encoder rerank top-50 → keep top-5/10. - **Budget**: MS MARCO MiniLM (fast, good quality). - **Quality**: Cohere Rerank or larger cross-encoders. - **Hard queries**: LLM rerank as fallback, not default. Core idea The Problem with Fixed-Size Chunking Fixed-size chunking (e.g., 512 tokens with 50 token overlap) is simple but semantically blind: Semantic Chunking: Split by Meaning Semantic chunking uses embeddings to detect where topics change: --- The Algorithm Step 1: Split Text into Sentences Step 2: Embed Sentence Windows Step 3: Calculate Similarity Between Adjacent Windows Step 4: Find Breakpoints and Create Chunks Complete Semantic Chunker --- Threshold Methods Compared | Method | How It Works | Best For | | -------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | | **Percentile** | Top X% of distances become breakpoints | Consistent chunk count | | **Stddev** | Mean + X standard deviations | Adaptive to document variation | | **Fixed** | Absolute distance threshold | When you know your data well | Tuning Recommendations | Document Type | Method | Threshold | Expected Chunk Size | | --------------- | ---------- | --------- | ------------------- | | News articles | Percentile | 0.90 | 3-5 paragraphs | | Technical docs | Percentile | 0.85 | 2-4 paragraphs | | Legal contracts | Stddev | 1.5 | Clause-level | | Conversations | Percentile | 0.95 | Topic turns | --- LangChain Implementation --- Failure modes ❌ Chunks Too Small Very low threshold creates many tiny chunks. - **Symptom**: Hundreds of 1-2 sentence chunks - **Fix**: Increase threshold or use percentile method ❌ Chunks Too Large Very high threshold rarely triggers breakpoints. - **Symptom**: Entire document becomes one chunk - **Fix**: Lower threshold or add size limits ❌ Slow Processing Embedding every sentence is expensive. - **Symptom**: Minutes per document - **Fix**: Use faster model (MiniLM) or batch embedding ❌ Not Respecting Document Structure Semantic chunking may split tables, code blocks, or lists. - **Fix**: Pre-split on structural boundaries, then apply semantic chunking to prose sections --- Production defaults | Setting | Recommended Value | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | **Embedding model** | all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (fast) or text-embedding-3-small | | **Window size** | 2-3 sentences | | **Threshold method** | Percentile | | **Threshold value** | 85-95 (depending on granularity needs) | | **Max chunk size** | Add hard cap (e.g., 2000 tokens) | | **Min chunk size** | Merge tiny chunks ( Combine semantic chunking with size limits. Core idea The Chunking Dilemma When building RAG systems, you face a fundamental trade-off: | Chunk Size | Embedding Precision | Context Completeness | | ------------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------- | | **Small** (1-2 sentences) | ✅ High | ❌ Low | | **Large** (paragraphs) | ❌ Low | ✅ High | **Small chunks** embed better because they capture a single concept. But when retrieved, they lack the surrounding context needed for the LLM to generate good answers. **Large chunks** provide more context but may contain multiple topics, diluting the embedding and causing retrieval misses. Sentence-Window Retrieval: Best of Both Worlds The solution: **embed small units, but retrieve larger windows**. Implementation Choosing Window Size | Document Type | Recommended Window | Rationale | | ---------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | **Legal/Technical** | 3-5 sentences | Context is critical for interpretation | | **News/Articles** | 2-3 sentences | Each sentence is more self-contained | | **Chat/Dialogue** | 4-6 turns | Conversation context is essential | | **Code Documentation** | 1-2 sentences + code block | Keep code with its description | Production defaults LlamaIndex Implementation Failure modes ❌ Window Too Small If your window size is 0 (sentence only), the LLM lacks context to generate coherent answers. ❌ Window Too Large If your window is huge (entire document), you lose the precision benefits and may hit token limits. ❌ Breaking Semantic Boundaries Naive sentence splitting can break: - Tables (rows become separate sentences) - Lists (items lose their header) - Code blocks (split on periods in code) Use a parser that respects document structure. ❌ Not Deduplicating Overlaps If two adjacent sentences both match, their windows overlap heavily. searchText: FLARE: Active Retrieval Retrieve dynamically during generation based on model confidence. retrieval flare active-retrieval iterative-rag confidence Understand FLARE's confidence-based retrieval triggers. Implement active retrieval during generation. Know when active retrieval improves vs complicates. Goals - Understand FLARE's approach to active retrieval. - Implement confidence-based retrieval triggers. - Build generation loops that retrieve on demand. Prereqs - Read: **Speculative RAG** (understand parallel approaches). Core idea What is FLARE? From Jiang et al., 2023: FLARE (Forward-Looking Active REtrieval) interleaves generation with retrieval: 1. Generate a sentence 2. Check confidence in generated tokens 3. If low confidence → retrieve relevant information 4. Continue generation with new context Why active retrieval helps | Scenario | Traditional RAG | FLARE | |----------|-----------------|-------| | Multi-hop question | May miss later hops | Retrieves as needed | | Long generation | Early context may be stale | Fresh retrieval | | Uncertain facts | Hallucinates | Retrieves to verify | Implementation Simplified FLARE (sentence-level) When to use FLARE | Use Case | FLARE Appropriate? | |----------|-------------------| | Multi-hop reasoning | ✓ Yes | | Evolving topics | ✓ Yes | | Long-form generation | ✓ Yes | | Simple Q&A | ✗ No (overkill) | | Streaming required | ~ Complex | Failure modes 1. **Retrieval loops**: Low confidence → bad retrieval → still low confidence. 2. **Slow generation**: Multiple retrievals add latency. 3. **Context bloat**: Accumulated context exceeds window. 4. **Over-retrieval**: Retrieving when not needed. Production defaults - **Confidence threshold**: 0.5-0.7 (tune on your data). - **Max iterations**: 5-10 sentences. - **Context management**: Summarize or truncate old context. - **Use for**: Complex queries, not simple lookups.
